lesson.title: Unraveling the Fold: How Proteins Lose Their Shape
lesson.summary: Denaturation is the disruption of a protein's secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure by heat, extreme pH, or other harsh conditions, and because it leaves the peptide bonds of the primary sequence intact while destroying everything the protein's shape depended on, it almost always destroys its function too.
lesson.body:
Denaturation is what happens when the noncovalent interactions holding a protein's higher-order structure in place get overwhelmed, causing the protein to unfold. Crucially, denaturation does not usually break the peptide bonds that make up the primary sequence, the covalent backbone stays connected. What is lost is the hydrogen bonding of secondary structure, the hydrophobic clustering and ionic interactions of tertiary structure, and any quaternary arrangement of subunits. Because a protein's three-dimensional shape is what allows it to bind a substrate, catalyze a reaction, or interact with another molecule, losing that shape almost always means losing that function, even though every amino acid is technically still present in the same order.

A number of conditions can trigger denaturation. Heat adds kinetic energy to a protein's atoms, which can shake apart the relatively weak hydrogen bonds and disrupt the hydrophobic packing that hold the folded structure together. Extreme pH, whether strongly acidic or strongly basic, changes the protonation state of acidic and basic side chains, which disrupts the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonding patterns those side chains would otherwise form, since the charge each side chain carries depends directly on the surrounding pH. Heavy metal ions, certain organic solvents, and denaturing chemicals such as urea can have similar effects, and even vigorous mechanical agitation can be enough to unfold some proteins.

Cooking an egg is a familiar, visible demonstration of denaturation. Raw egg white is mostly a solution of the protein ovalbumin folded into a compact, soluble tertiary structure. Heating the egg disrupts that folding, exposing hydrophobic regions of the protein that were previously tucked safely in the interior. Those newly exposed hydrophobic patches on different unfolded protein molecules stick to each other, and the proteins aggregate into a solid, opaque network, which is why a clear, runny egg white turns into a white, rubbery solid when cooked. It is worth noting this is chemically distinct from digestion, which breaks the covalent peptide bonds of primary structure through hydrolysis rather than simply unfolding the protein.

Denaturation is not always permanent. In a well known set of experiments, biochemist Christian Anfinsen showed that the enzyme ribonuclease A, after being fully denatured with urea and a reducing agent that broke its disulfide bonds, could spontaneously refold back into its correct, active shape once those denaturing conditions were removed. This demonstrated that the primary sequence alone contains enough information to specify the protein's correct tertiary structure, without any outside instructions. Still, many denaturation events, like the aggregated proteins in a cooked egg, are effectively irreversible.

Denaturation also has direct relevance inside the human body. Digestion begins in the stomach partly through denaturation: the strongly acidic environment there, around pH 2, unfolds dietary proteins, exposing the peptide bonds that digestive enzymes then hydrolyze. Fever illustrates the same chemistry from a different angle, a body temperature that climbs too high risks denaturing essential enzymes, which is part of why sustained high fevers are medically dangerous rather than simply uncomfortable.
